The Erdzeichen is an artwork on the grounds of Munich Airport by the painter Wilhelm Holderied and the sculptor Karl Schlamminger. According to the artist, the earth sculpture at the airport is meant to be “An Island in Time,” i.e. a symbol of time sequences which are determined by the “primeval energy of the earth.” The ground-level artwork was completed in 1995. It stands in the tradition of archaic earth sculptures and modern works of Land Art, and also calls to mind Smithson’s famous “Spiral Jetty.” The Earthsign stretches across an area measuring 270 meters by 170 meters. Its furrows are 3.40 meters deep. These furrows and the tall gravel embankments between them circle a central point, continue in a straight row, form a loop and then flow in irregularly undulating lines into the surrounding field, where they end at a straight line. The artwork was paid for by about 400 donors in a campaign entitled “Be Part of Art.” The aerial archaeological photographer Klaus Leidorf has documented the earth sculpture and the changes which nature and the seasons have brought to it since 1994.

Eremophila is a group of more than 270 types of plants that all grow only in mainland Australia. They belong to the figwort family, called Scrophulariaceae. Some Eremophila plants have common names like emu bush, poverty bush, or fuchsia bush. These names come from ideas like emus eating their fruit, living in dry places, or looking a little like fuchsia flowers. Eremophilasgrow in many dry parts of Australia and can be small bushes or small trees. They grow in every mainland state, but there are the most kinds in Western Australia. Their petals are joined together at least at the base, forming a tube. The top petals look different from the bottom ones. Eremophila plants can be very different in size and shape. Some are low and spread out like E. serpens, while others are small trees like E. bignoniiflora. Their leaves also change in size and shape but are usually small and can be shiny or hairy. Their flowers usually have five sepals that spread out and five petals joined into a tube at the base. The flowers are often red, purple, lilac, or mauve, but some are white or green. Many flowers have mixed colors or spots and stripes. Sometimes only the petals have color, but often the sepals do too. The flower shapes vary. Most have two petals on top of the tube and three below, with stamens inside the tube, like E. exilifolia. These flowers are usually pollinated by insects, and the lower petals help insects land. Some flowers have four petals on top and one curled under, with stamens sticking out, like E. glabra. These are usually pollinated by birds, which hold the plant while they feed. A few flowers have a mix of these shapes. When the flower gets old, the petals fall off. Then the calyx (the outer part) grows bigger and changes color as the fruit grows. The fruit has 2 to 12 seeds and can stay in the ground for many years until something like fire, heavy rain, or human work like road building wakes them up. Some plants, like E. sturtii, can grow new shoots from roots and sometimes become weeds. But many Eremophila plants are rare or in danger because of things people do, like clearing land, farming, and mining. The group of plants called Eremophila was first officially described in 1810 by a scientist named Robert Brown. He named the first two species E. oppositifolia and E. alternifolia but did not choose one main species to represent the group. Later, Ferdinand von Mueller, a botanist from Victoria, studied this group a lot and described 47 species. He found many of these plants during trips to remote parts of Australia. Today, Robert Chinnock is the expert who has named over 100 species of Eremophila. Because many plants grow in hard-to-reach places, there are still more species to be named. So far, 221 species have been described, and 40 more have been found but not yet officially named. The newest species added were Eremophila buirchellii and Eremophila calcicola, described in 2016. The name Eremophila comes from ancient Greek words: ἐρῆμος (erêmos) meaning "lonely" or "desert," and φίλος (phílos) meaning "dear" or "beloved." This name shows that these plants love living in dry, desert-like places. In 2021, scientists did a big study using molecular data (looking at DNA) to understand how different Eremophila species are related to each other and to other plants in the same tribe called Myoporeae. They studied 205 out of 233 known species of Eremophila at that time. The study found that a plant from the Caribbean called Bontia daphnoides actually belongs inside the Eremophila group. The family tree they made shows four main groups (called clades). It also shows that the whole Eremophila group is paraphyletic, meaning it includes some but not all descendants, because other related plant groups like Myoporum, Bontia, Glycocystis, Pentacoelium, Calamphoreus and Diocirea are inside it. Even though Bontia daphnoides is from the Caribbean, it is deeply connected to one of these groups (clade C). Scientists have ideas on how to fix this classification, but no changes have been made yet. Many eremophilas are called emu bush or poverty bush as part of their common names. Sometimes two species have the same common name and sometimes one species has more than one common name. Of the approximately 270 species, the following have at least one common name: E. bignoniiflora – gooramurra, bignonia emu bush E. gilesii – Charleville turkey bush, green turkey bush, Giles emu bush E. scoparia – silver emu bush, broom bush E. campanulata – bell-flowered poverty bush E. granitica – granite poverty bush, thin-leaved poverty bush E. micrantha – small-flowered poverty bush E. parvifolia – small-leaved poverty bush E. pterocarpa – wing-fruited eremophila, silver poverty bush Eremophilas grow all over mainland Australia, mostly in dry areas. Most types are found in Western Australia. One species, Eremophila maculata, grows in every Australian state except Tasmania, where no Eremophilas live. Eremophila debilis is found in New Zealand, but it probably got there recently because people brought it. There are at least 229 species in Western Australia, and about 80% of these only grow there. They are very common in dry places. For example, in the Meekatharra-Wiluna area, there are more than 50 kinds of Eremophilas, and they are the most common small bushes. Some species, like E. complanata and E. mirabilis, grow only in one or two small rocky places. Eremophila plants have flowers that attract either insects or birds. Flowers that attract insects usually have a lower lip that sticks out so insects can land on it. These flowers are often blue, purple, or white. Flowers that attract birds are red, orange, yellow, or green and have parts that point down to keep insects away. Bird-pollinated flowers also have long stamens that brush pollen onto the bird’s head when it feeds. Emus eat the fruits of Eremophila and spread the seeds in their droppings. However, it is not true that this helps the seeds to start growing. Some plants, like E.freelingii and E.latrobei, are poisonous to farm animals. But others, such as E.bignoniiflora and E.oppositifolia, can be used as food for animals. Indigenous Australians used eremophilas in their culture and health. For example, the Adnyamathanha people used a plant called Varti-varka (Eremophila longifolia) in burial and initiation ceremonies. They also treated skin problems with a mix of emu oil and ash made from burning the plant’s bark. Scientists are now studying the chemicals in these plants to understand how they help with health.. In the past, eremophilas were not often used in gardens, though some types like Eremophila maculata were known. This was because they were hard to grow from seeds or cuttings and were not common even in nature. But now, as growing methods have improved, eremophilas have become much more popular. They have beautiful flowers, different kinds of leaves, and bloom for a long time, making them good garden plants. They mostly need little water and can handle frost, so they can grow in many places. Growing eremophilas from seeds is hard because the seeds need special care, like staying in the ground for a long time or being carefully taken out of the fruit. Many plants are grown by grafting them onto roots of Myoporum plants, which helps them grow in almost any soil, even heavy clay. Different Myoporum species are used depending on the garden location. Eremophilas naturally grow in dry parts of Australia where it rains very little. They can survive long dry times or droughts lasting years. This makes them great for gardens that need little care or where water is limited. Too much water can harm many eremophila plants, so they can be hard to grow in wet areas or places with poor drainage, like parts of Eastern Australia. In gardens, they should be watered regularly for the first 1-2 years and given native plant fertilizer. Some species, like E. microtheca, may lose their leaves during very dry times and look dead, but they can recover and grow well after deep watering.

An ergastic substance is a non-protoplasm material that one can find in cells. These are usually products of metabolism. Ergastic substances include crystals, oil drops, gums, tannins, resins and other compounds. Some of these substances help the organism function, keep up cell structure, or are just stored food material such as oil or fat. During the life of a cell, they can appear and disappear. Ergastic substances may appear in the protoplasm, in vacuoles, or in the cell wall. Ergastic substances are usually absent in tissue with dividing cells, such as meristem tissue in plants. Plant cells often store noxious substances in leaf cells as a kind of defence against herbivory. In animals storing noxious substances is done as defence against predation. Storing venom for use in biting or stings is common in some groups of animals. In general, if animals need quantity of a liquid substance they produce it with special cells in a gland, and send the product to where it is needed or stored.
